note:
Ambient scribe transcript. Gynecology specialty clinic follow-up visit for a 40-year-old female with chronic pelvic pain.

Doctor: Good to see you again. How has the pelvic pain been since the last visit?
Patient: About the same. It's a dull ache low in my belly, and it gets much worse right before and during my period.
Doctor: Any pain with intercourse?
Patient: Yes, deep pain with sex, so we mostly avoid it.
Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, or blood in your urine?
Patient: No fever, no discharge, and no blood in my urine.
Doctor: How is the ibuprofen working for you?
Patient: Ibuprofen 600 mg three times a day with food takes the edge off for a few hours. I still miss work on the worst days.
Doctor: Your pelvic ultrasound last month showed no ovarian cyst and no fibroids, and your pregnancy test was negative.
Patient: Okay. The hard part is getting here. I rely on a bus that only runs twice a day, so I miss a lot of appointments.
Doctor: I understand. On exam today your abdomen is soft, there is tenderness in the lower pelvis on the left side, and I feel a tender nodularity behind the uterus. No masses. Your vital signs are normal.
Doctor: My impression is chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. We will keep the ibuprofen and start norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily to suppress your periods. I will order a pelvic MRI and schedule it close to your next visit so you only make one trip, and I will arrange that follow-up as a video visit in 3 months.
Patient: That would help a lot. Thank you.
summary: A 40-year-old female was seen in a gynecology specialty clinic for follow-up of chronic pelvic pain that worsens around her periods, with deep pain during sex. She denied fever, vaginal discharge, and blood in her urine, and ibuprofen gives only partial relief. A pelvic ultrasound last month showed no ovarian cyst or fibroids and a pregnancy test was negative, while the exam found left lower pelvic tenderness and tender nodularity behind the uterus. The impression is chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. The plan is to continue ibuprofen, start norethindrone acetate, order a pelvic MRI, and hold a video follow-up in 3 months because bus transportation makes visits difficult.

Transportation is a barrier: she relies on a bus that runs only twice a day and misses many appointments.

soap.assessment: Chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis.

Start norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily to suppress periods
Order pelvic MRI, scheduled close to the next visit so she makes only one trip

note:
Hospital day 2 on the family medicine ward for a 38-year-old female admitted yesterday evening for observation after an episode of intense sneezing, nasal congestion, and lightheadedness at home during peak pollen season. She has had itchy, watery eyes and clear rhinorrhea every spring for several years, and this week the symptoms were much worse after yard work. She denies wheezing, throat tightness, hives, and fever. Overnight she had no further lightheadedness and slept well. This morning she has only mild nasal stuffiness. She has no known drug allergies.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 98.4 F, BP 118/72, HR 76, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air. Examination showed pale, boggy nasal turbinates with clear drainage, mildly injected conjunctivae, and a clear oropharynx. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally without wheeze. There was no urticaria on skin exam.

Impression: seasonal allergic rhinitis, now improved, with no evidence of anaphylaxis. I started fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, and loratadine 10 mg once daily. She was advised to shower and change clothes after outdoor exposure and to keep windows closed on high pollen days. She is medically ready for discharge today, with follow-up in the family medicine clinic in 2 weeks and an allergy referral if symptoms persist.

note: Dictating a nephrology clinic follow-up on an 85-year-old female who is on in-center hemodialysis three times a week for end-stage renal disease. She comes in today because she has been about 3 kilograms over her target weight at the start of her last two sessions, and she has noticed swelling in both ankles and more shortness of breath when she walks to the mailbox. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, and fever, and she admits she has been drinking more fluids and eating canned soups. Her only other chronic problem is hypertension. Vital signs today blood pressure 156/84, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. On exam she has bibasilar crackles, 2 plus pitting edema to the knees, and jugular venous distension, no pericardial rub. Labs from her last session show potassium 4.6 and hemoglobin 10.4. Assessment is fluid overload from excess interdialytic weight gain in a hemodialysis patient with end-stage renal disease. Plan is to lower her target dry weight by 1 kilogram and add an extra ultrafiltration session this week, correction, make that an extra full dialysis session this week. Counsel her on a 1 liter daily fluid restriction and a 2 gram sodium diet, continue amlodipine 5 mg daily, and have the dietitian see her. Get a chest x-ray if the crackles persist. Return to clinic in 2 weeks.

note:
Neuro ward, HD#2. 21-year-old male w/ T1DM x 9 yrs, admitted via ED w/ worsening burning pain in both feet.

CC: burning/stabbing pain in feet x 4 mo, worse at night, 8/10, can't sleep. Numbness up to ankles bilat. Tingling in toes.
Denies leg weakness, falls, back pain, bowel or bladder incontinence, visual changes, fever.
No foot ulcers per pt.
PMH: T1DM dx age 12, microalbuminuria. No known retinopathy.
SH: works part-time, no insurance. Rationing meds d/t cost. No alcohol, no tobacco.

Home meds per pt at admission:
- insulin glargine 30 u qHS
- lispro w/ meals
- lisinopril 5 mg daily
- pregabalin 75 mg BID, stopped ~6 wks ago (cost)
CORRECTION after bottle review + pharmacy call: glargine Rx is 24 u qHS, not 30. Pt has been taking only ~12 u to stretch vials. Pregabalin Rx was 150 mg BID, not 75. Lispro Rx is 6 u TID w/ meals.

Vitals: BP 128/78, HR 84, RR 16, Temp 98.6 F, SpO2 99% RA.
Exam: A&Ox3, CN II-XII intact. Strength 5/5 all 4 ext. Ankle reflexes absent bilat, patellar 1+. Decr pinprick + vibration to mid-shin bilat, monofilament absent at toes bilat. Proprioception intact. Romberg neg. No foot ulcers or calluses. DP/PT pulses 2+ bilat. Gait cautious, no ataxia.

Data:
Glucose 342 on admit, A1c 11.4%.
Na 138, K 4.2, Cr 0.9.
B12 520, TSH 1.8.
UACR 85 mg/g.
NCS/EMG: reduced sural + peroneal sensory amplitudes bilat, mildly slowed conduction velocity, c/w length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
MRI L-spine: no canal stenosis, no cord lesion.

Impression: painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, length-dependent, w/ poorly controlled T1DM (A1c 11.4%). Med non-adherence d/t cost is main driver. B12 def and thyroid dz unlikely.

Plan:
- D/c pregabalin from med list (unaffordable, not taking)
- Start gabapentin 300 mg qHS, titrate to 300 mg TID by HD#4 if tolerated. Counsel re sedation, dizziness
- Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN pain
- Cont insulin glargine 24 u qHS and insulin lispro 6 u TID w/ meals
- Cont lisinopril 5 mg daily
- SW + pharmacy consult for cost assistance / generic options
- Endo consult, diabetes educator
- Daily foot checks, podiatry referral
- Repeat A1c in 3 mo
- F/u neuro clinic 4 wks
- Anticipate d/c HD#4 if pain < 4/10

note:
Ambient scribe transcript. Gastroenterology specialty clinic follow-up visit for a 66-year-old female with celiac disease.

Doctor: Good to see you. It has been about a year since your celiac diagnosis. How are you feeling?
Patient: Better than before, but I still get bloated after meals sometimes, and I'm tired a lot.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, belly pain, or weight loss?
Patient: No diarrhea, no belly pain, and my weight has been steady.
Doctor: Any black stools or blood in your stool, since you take a blood thinner?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: How strict have you been with the gluten-free diet?
Patient: Pretty strict at home. When we eat out I'm not always sure, so I probably get some cross-contact.
Doctor: That's common. What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day for my atrial fibrillation, ferrous sulfate 325 mg every day, and a vitamin D supplement.
Doctor: Any trouble with the iron?
Patient: It gives me constipation.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 126/74, heart rate 72 and a bit irregular, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. On exam your abdomen is soft, not tender, and not distended, and I don't see any rash. Your labs from last week show a hemoglobin of 11.2 and a ferritin of 14. Your tissue transglutaminase antibody is still mildly elevated, though much lower than at diagnosis.
Patient: So is the celiac still active?
Doctor: It means some gluten is still getting in, and the low ferritin tells us your iron stores are still low. My impression is celiac disease with ongoing mild gluten exposure, iron-deficiency anemia, and your atrial fibrillation is stable on the apixaban. For the iron, let's change the ferrous sulfate to 325 mg every other day, which absorbs better and is easier on the bowels. Continue the apixaban and the vitamin D. I want you to meet with our dietitian about eating out safely. I'll order a repeat upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsies, and we'll coordinate with your cardiologist about holding the apixaban for a short time before the procedure. Come back in 3 months.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good.
summary: A 66-year-old female with celiac disease and atrial fibrillation on apixaban was seen for follow-up and reported residual bloating and fatigue, with no diarrhea, belly pain, weight loss, or black or bloody stools. She admits possible cross-contact when eating out and has constipation from her iron. Exam was benign, with hemoglobin 11.2, ferritin 14, and a still mildly elevated tissue transglutaminase antibody. The impression is celiac disease with ongoing mild gluten exposure and iron-deficiency anemia. Ferrous sulfate is changed to every other day, a dietitian visit and repeat upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsies are planned, and the apixaban hold will be coordinated with cardiology, with follow-up in 3 months.

note:
Ambient scribe transcript. Neurology outpatient clinic visit for an 80-year-old female referred after a first seizure. Her daughter is also present.

Doctor: Tell me what happened ten days ago.
Family member: I found her on the kitchen floor. Her whole body was stiff and then jerking for maybe two minutes. Her lips looked blue for a little while.
Patient: I don't remember any of it. I woke up in the ambulance, confused, and my tongue was sore.
Doctor: Did you have any warning, like a strange smell, a funny feeling, or dizziness?
Patient: No warning at all.
Doctor: Any head injury, fever, or recent illness?
Patient: No head injury, no fever, and I wasn't sick.
Doctor: Have you ever had a seizure before?
Patient: Never.
Doctor: Did she lose control of her bladder?
Family member: No, she didn't wet herself.
Doctor: Any alcohol, or any new medicines?
Patient: No alcohol and no new medicines. I take amlodipine 5 mg daily for my blood pressure and atorvastatin 20 mg at night.
Doctor: In the emergency department, the CT of your head showed no bleeding and no mass, and your blood sugar and sodium were normal. The MRI of your brain showed old small vessel disease but no tumor and no new stroke. The EEG showed some sharp waves over the left temporal area.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: It means a part of the brain is irritable and could cause another seizure. Today your blood pressure is 138/76 and heart rate is 68. You are alert and oriented, your speech is fluent, strength and sensation are normal, and your walking is steady.
Doctor: My impression is a first unprovoked seizure. Because of the abnormal EEG and the small vessel changes, another seizure is more likely, so I recommend starting levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day. Continue amlodipine and atorvastatin as you are taking them. No driving, no bathing alone, and avoid ladders. Call 911 if a seizure lasts more than five minutes. I would like to see you again in 6 weeks.
Family member: We will make sure she takes it every day.
summary: An 80-year-old female was seen in neurology clinic after a witnessed episode of stiffening and jerking for about two minutes with confusion and a sore tongue afterward, with no warning, head injury, fever, or incontinence. She takes amlodipine and atorvastatin and drinks no alcohol. CT of the head showed no bleeding or mass, MRI showed old small vessel disease, and EEG showed left temporal sharp waves, with a normal neurologic exam. The impression is a first unprovoked seizure with a higher recurrence risk. Levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day is started, seizure precautions are given, and follow-up is in 6 weeks.

The patient does not remember it, woke in the ambulance confused, and her tongue was sore. No warning, no head injury, no fever, no illness, no bladder incontinence, and no prior seizures. No alcohol and no new medicines; takes amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg at night.

EEG: sharp waves over the left temporal area. Today blood pressure 138/76, heart rate 68. Alert and oriented, fluent speech, normal strength and sensation, steady gait.
soap.assessment: First unprovoked seizure; with the abnormal EEG and small vessel changes another seizure is more likely.
plan: Start levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day
Continue amlodipine and atorvastatin

note:
Ambient scribe transcript. Gastroenterology outpatient clinic, new visit for a 51-year-old female with trouble swallowing.

Doctor: Thanks for coming in. Tell me about the swallowing problem.
Patient: It started about three months ago. At first it was just steak and bread getting stuck, but now even rice and pills feel like they stop in the middle of my chest. Last week I had trouble with soup too.
Doctor: Is it getting worse over time?
Patient: Yes, steadily worse. I've also lost about twelve pounds without trying.
Doctor: Any pain when you swallow, or food coming back up?
Patient: Sometimes food comes back up after meals, and I cough when I eat. No pain with swallowing, though.
Doctor: Any vomiting blood, black stools, chest pain, or hoarseness?
Patient: No blood, no black stools, no chest pain, and my voice is normal.
Doctor: I see you were in the hospital recently.
Patient: Yes, about three weeks ago for pneumonia. They said food went into my lung. I got IV antibiotics for five days, then took pills at home, and I finished those last week.
Doctor: Do you have a fever now, or still coughing a lot?
Patient: No fever. The cough is much better.
Doctor: Good. And your medical history?
Patient: Acid reflux for years, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and an underactive thyroid.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Omeprazole 40 mg once a day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, lisinopril 10 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 micrograms in the morning, and ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a week for back aches.
Doctor: Let me double check the omeprazole dose. Can you look at the bottle?
Patient: Sorry, let me see. It says 20 mg, not 40. So I take 20 mg once a day.
Doctor: Thank you, that is what I will document. Your vital signs today are blood pressure 132/80 and heart rate 78, and your weight is 148 pounds, which is 12 pounds down from your last visit. Your throat looks clear, there are no lumps in the neck, your lungs are clear, and your abdomen is soft without any mass. During your hospital stay the chest x-ray showed pneumonia in the right lower lobe, and your hemoglobin at discharge was 11.8. The barium swallow done in the hospital showed narrowing in the lower esophagus with slow passage of food.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: With reflux that has gone on for years, I am concerned about a stricture, which is scarring in the esophagus, and I cannot rule out a tumor, so we need to look directly. My impression is progressive dysphagia, most likely from an esophageal stricture, with recent aspiration pneumonia. I want an upper endoscopy, an EGD, within a week, with biopsies and dilation if it is a stricture. Until then, eat soft and pureed foods, take small bites, and sit upright for 30 minutes after meals. Stop the ibuprofen completely, since it can irritate the esophagus, and use acetaminophen if you need something for your back. Increase the omeprazole to 40 mg twice a day. Continue the metformin, lisinopril, and levothyroxine at the same doses. I will also refer you to a dietitian, and I will see you two weeks after the procedure.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: A 51-year-old female with reflux, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hypothyroidism was seen for three months of progressive dysphagia, now with food regurgitation, cough with meals, and a 12-pound weight loss. She was hospitalized three weeks ago for aspiration pneumonia, and she denied pain with swallowing, vomiting blood, black stools, chest pain, hoarseness, and fever. Her omeprazole dose was clarified as 20 mg once daily. Barium swallow showed lower esophageal narrowing, and the impression is progressive dysphagia, most likely from an esophageal stricture. Plan is an upper endoscopy within a week with biopsies and possible dilation, stopping ibuprofen, increasing omeprazole to 40 mg twice daily, a soft diet, and a dietitian referral.

note:
Ambient scribe transcript. Gastroenterology outpatient clinic, evaluation of anemia in a 20-year-old female.

Doctor: Your primary care doctor sent you because your blood count showed low iron. What have you noticed?
Patient: I've been exhausted for months, and I get dizzy when I stand up fast. My friends say I look pale. I also keep craving ice, which sounds weird.
Doctor: How does your work schedule fit into this?
Patient: I work nights at a distribution center, three or four nights a week, but the schedule changes every week and sometimes they switch me to days. My sleep and my meals are all over the place.
Doctor: Any black or bloody stools?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Belly pain, diarrhea, or trouble swallowing?
Patient: No belly pain, no diarrhea, and swallowing is fine.
Doctor: Any weight loss?
Patient: No, my weight is the same.
Doctor: Tell me about your periods.
Patient: They are heavy. They last about seven days, and I soak a pad every two or three hours on the first two days, with some clots.
Doctor: What are you taking?
Patient: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice a day, omeprazole 20 mg every morning that I bought over the counter for heartburn, ibuprofen 400 mg when I get a migraine, sertraline 100 mg daily, and my albuterol inhaler for asthma.
Doctor: Let's go through the iron again. Twice a day?
Patient: Sorry, no. I only take the iron once a day, and I skip it on nights when I am rushing to work.
Doctor: And the sertraline? My list shows 50 mg.
Patient: Let me look at the bottle. You are right, it is 50 mg once a day.
Doctor: Thank you. Your vital signs today are blood pressure 104/62, heart rate 96, and oxygen saturation 99 percent. You look pale and your conjunctivae are pale. Your heart rhythm is regular with a soft flow murmur, your lungs are clear, and your abdomen is soft and not tender, with no liver or spleen enlargement. Your labs from last week show a hemoglobin of 9.1, an MCV of 74, and a ferritin of 6, which confirms iron deficiency. The celiac antibody, tissue transglutaminase IgA, was negative with a normal total IgA, and your pregnancy test was negative.
Patient: So what is causing it?
Doctor: My impression is iron-deficiency anemia, most likely from your heavy periods, but we also need to rule out a bleeding or absorption problem in the gut. The omeprazole and the ibuprofen can both make this worse, since the acid blocker reduces iron absorption and ibuprofen can irritate the stomach and cause bleeding. So I would like you to stop the omeprazole and the ibuprofen. For migraines you can use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed, and tell me if the heartburn comes back.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: For the iron, change the ferrous sulfate to 325 mg every other day, taken with water on an empty stomach at the start of your day, whatever your day is, even if that is after a night shift. Keep the sertraline 50 mg daily and the albuterol as needed.
Patient: Does it matter that I am asleep during the day?
Doctor: Take the iron when you wake up, away from coffee or tea. I am going to order an upper endoscopy with biopsies of the stomach and small bowel, and a stool test for H. pylori. We will schedule the endoscopy on a day off or right after a night shift, whichever you prefer, so you are not losing sleep. I will refer you to gynecology for the heavy periods, and we will repeat the blood count and ferritin in 8 weeks. If the hemoglobin does not improve, we will consider a colonoscopy and IV iron.
Patient: Okay, I will text the scheduler with my shifts.

She denied black or bloody stools, belly pain, diarrhea, swallowing trouble, and weight loss. Hemoglobin was 9.1, MCV 74, and ferritin 6, with a negative celiac antibody and pregnancy test, and exam showed pallor and a soft flow murmur. The impression is iron-deficiency anemia, most likely from heavy periods, with a gut source still to be excluded. Omeprazole and ibuprofen are stopped, iron is changed to every other day, and an upper endoscopy with biopsies, an H. pylori stool test, and a gynecology referral are planned.

note:
Nephrology telehealth note. Real-time video visit, patient connected from home with a stable connection and has a home blood pressure cuff and scale.

The patient is a 76-year-old female on in-center hemodialysis three times a week for end-stage renal disease. She reports ankle swelling and shortness of breath when climbing stairs over the last week. She works irregular rotating shifts as a home health aide and has missed or shortened her last two dialysis sessions because of schedule conflicts. Her home scale shows about 2.5 kg above her dry weight. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, and fever. Her only other chronic problem is hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 5 mg daily.

Home readings: BP 152/88, heart rate 80. On video she is comfortable and speaks in full sentences, with visible bilateral ankle swelling and no increased work of breathing. Lung sounds cannot be assessed by video.

Impression: fluid overload related to missed and shortened dialysis sessions in a hemodialysis patient. Recommendations: add an extra dialysis session this week and keep all sessions full length. She should go to the emergency department for worsening shortness of breath or chest pain. Repeat video visit in 1 week.

Gastroenterology telehealth note. Real-time video visit; the patient, a 28-year-old male, joined from home, confirmed his identity and location, and consented to a telehealth visit. Reason for visit: follow-up of iron-deficiency anemia found on labs ordered by his primary care provider.

History: He reports 3 months of fatigue and decreased exercise tolerance, along with mild burning epigastric discomfort after meals that is worse when he takes ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a week for knee pain from running. He noticed small amounts of bright red blood on the toilet paper twice in the past month. He denies black stools, vomiting, abdominal pain at rest, diarrhea, weight loss, and trouble swallowing. He eats a regular diet that includes meat and has no prior GI problems.

Results reviewed: hemoglobin 10.2, MCV 72, ferritin 8. Tissue transglutaminase IgA was negative.

Home readings: BP 118/72, heart rate 88, home weight 78 kg. On video he appears mildly pale but in no distress, speaks in full sentences, and has no visible jaundice. He pressed on his upper abdomen himself and reports no tenderness. A hands-on abdominal exam was not possible by video.

Impression: iron-deficiency anemia, likely from slow gastrointestinal blood loss, with NSAID-associated dyspepsia and small-volume hematochezia that is probably hemorrhoidal. Celiac disease is less likely with the negative serology.

Recommendations: Start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily with water. Stop ibuprofen; use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain. Order an EGD and a colonoscopy with biopsies. Repeat CBC and ferritin in 4 weeks. He should call or go to the emergency department for black stools, heavy bleeding, or fainting. Video follow-up after the procedures.

note:
Ambient scribe transcript. Urgent care visit for a 7-year-old female with wheezing and trouble breathing, accompanied by her mother.

Doctor: What brought her in today?
Family member: She has been coughing and wheezing since last night, and this morning she was breathing really fast and could barely finish a sentence. I gave her the albuterol inhaler every two or three hours and it only helps for a short time.
Doctor: When did this start?
Family member: She got a cold three days ago, runny nose and cough, and then yesterday we visited her grandmother's house, which has a cat.
Doctor: Any fever, vomiting, or chest pain?
Family member: No fever and no vomiting. She says her chest feels tight.
Doctor: Any rash, lip swelling, or choking on food before this started?
Family member: No rash, no swelling, and nothing like choking.
Doctor: Does she have other medical problems?
Family member: Asthma since she was little, eczema, and allergic rhinitis.
Doctor: What medicines does she take?
Family member: For asthma she uses fluticasone, the 220 micrograms, two puffs twice a day with the spacer, and albuterol when needed. She takes cetirizine 5 mg every day for her allergies. She was on montelukast 5 mg at night, but we stopped it two months ago because she had nightmares.
Doctor: Let's double check the fluticasone strength. Can you look at the inhaler?
Family member: Sorry, let me see. The box says 44 micrograms, not 220. So it is 44 micrograms, two puffs twice a day.
Doctor: Thank you. Does she miss doses?
Family member: Probably a few times a week, to be honest.
Doctor: Okay. Her triage vitals were temperature 98.9 F, heart rate 128, respiratory rate 32, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air. On exam she is sitting forward and speaking in short phrases, with wheezing throughout both lungs, a long expiratory phase, and mild retractions under the ribs. No rash and no swelling of the lips. Her ears and throat look normal apart from clear nasal drainage. I am going to give her albuterol with ipratropium by nebulizer, then two more albuterol treatments, and a steroid by mouth, and get a chest x-ray.
Family member: Okay, please help her.
Doctor: Re-checking her after three treatments: she is speaking in full sentences now, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, with only a little wheeze at the end of each breath and no retractions. The chest x-ray shows overinflated lungs but no pneumonia.
Family member: She looks so much better.
Doctor: My impression is an asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral cold and cat exposure, in a child with asthma, eczema, and allergic rhinitis. She received three albuterol nebulizer treatments, 2.5 mg each, one ipratropium nebulizer, 0.5 mg, and dexamethasone 13 mg by mouth. At home, give albuterol 4 puffs with the spacer every four hours for the next day, then as needed, and one more dose of dexamethasone 13 mg tomorrow. Because she misses doses and has needed more albuterol, increase the fluticasone to 110 micrograms, one puff twice a day with the spacer, and have her rinse her mouth afterward. Keep the montelukast stopped. Continue cetirizine 5 mg daily. Avoid cats. See her pediatrician in two days to review her asthma action plan. Come back or call 911 if she is breathing fast, cannot talk, or her lips turn blue.
Family member: Understood, thank you.
summary: A 7-year-old female with asthma, eczema, and allergic rhinitis presented to urgent care with a day of cough, wheezing, chest tightness, and fast breathing after a cold and cat exposure, with minimal relief from albuterol. She had no fever, vomiting, rash, lip swelling, or choking. Oxygen saturation was 91 percent with diffuse wheezing and retractions, improving to 96 percent after albuterol, ipratropium, and dexamethasone, and the chest x-ray showed no pneumonia. The impression is an asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral cold and cat exposure. Albuterol is continued at home, a second dexamethasone dose given, fluticasone increased to 110 micrograms twice a day, montelukast kept off, and pediatrician follow-up arranged in two days.

note:
Hospital day 3, endocrinology consult service, following this 74-year-old male admitted with symptomatic hypercalcemia from primary hyperparathyroidism.

Interval events: He was admitted two days ago with several weeks of fatigue, constipation, increased urination, and nausea, and became confused the evening before admission. The confusion has resolved since fluids were started. He denies chest pain, vomiting, bone pain, and fractures, and has had no fever. On admission he said he drinks "a couple of beers" in the evening; after repeat questioning today he clarified that he drinks 6 to 8 beers every night, and his last drink was the night before admission. He works rotating overnight security shifts, which makes his sleep and meal timing irregular. CIWA scores have stayed low and he has had no tremor or hallucinations.

Medical history includes hypertension, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, osteoporosis, and a kidney stone 5 years ago. Home medications on admission were hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and over-the-counter calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily. Hydrochlorothiazide and calcium carbonate were discontinued on admission because both raise calcium. Lisinopril is on hold because of the acute kidney injury. Normal saline was reduced today from 200 mL/hr to 125 mL/hr as calcium improved. He received calcitonin 320 units subcutaneously every 12 hours for the first 48 hours. Cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily was started yesterday. He is also receiving thiamine 100 mg daily and folic acid 1 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily was started for blood pressure after hydrochlorothiazide was stopped.

Today temperature 98.1 F, BP 142/84, HR 74, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with moist mucous membranes, no palpable neck mass, a regular rhythm, a soft nontender abdomen, and no tremor.

Data: calcium 11.4 mg/dL today, down from 13.8 on admission after correction for albumin. PTH 142 pg/mL, inappropriately elevated. Phosphorus 2.2, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 24, magnesium 1.6, potassium 3.9, sodium 136. Creatinine 1.6 (1.9 on admission, baseline 1.4), eGFR 43. AST 62, ALT 38, and lipase normal. Neck ultrasound showed a 1.8 cm hypoechoic nodule posterior to the left lower thyroid lobe consistent with a parathyroid adenoma, and a sestamibi scan showed concordant uptake in the left inferior position. Renal ultrasound showed a nonobstructing 4 mm stone in the right kidney. A bone density study last year showed a T-score of -3.1 at the distal radius.

Impression: primary hyperparathyroidism with symptomatic hypercalcemia from a left inferior parathyroid adenoma, improving. Acute kidney injury on stage 3 chronic kidney disease from hypercalcemia and volume depletion, improving. Alcohol use disorder with heavy nightly drinking and no withdrawal so far.

Plan: continue normal saline at 125 mL/hr and check calcium and creatinine every 12 hours. Continue cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily. No thiazides, calcium supplements, or vitamin D supplements. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and keep lisinopril on hold until creatinine returns to baseline. Continue thiamine and folic acid with CIWA monitoring. Endocrine surgery will see him tomorrow to plan parathyroidectomy. Addiction medicine consult and alcohol cessation counseling today. Social work will help schedule follow-up around his overnight shifts and give him a written medication schedule. Discharge when calcium is below 11 and he is eating and drinking well, with endocrinology follow-up in 1 week.
summary: A 74-year-old male with hypertension, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and osteoporosis is on hospital day 3 for symptomatic hypercalcemia from primary hyperparathyroidism, with improving calcium of 11.4 mg/dL and PTH 142. Imaging showed a left inferior parathyroid adenoma, and he clarified that he drinks 6 to 8 beers nightly, with no withdrawal so far. Hydrochlorothiazide and calcium carbonate were discontinued, saline was reduced to 125 mL/hr, and cinacalcet was started. Creatinine is improving from 1.9 to 1.6. Plan is continued fluids and 12-hourly labs, endocrine surgery review for parathyroidectomy, thiamine and folic acid with CIWA monitoring, addiction medicine, and discharge once calcium is below 11.

note:
Chief Complaint: Right flank pain.

HPI: 60-year-old female who presents with sudden-onset right flank pain radiating to the groin that began 4 hours ago, rated 9/10 and colicky, with nausea and one episode of vomiting. She reports blood in her urine. She has no significant past medical history. She denies fever, chills, dysuria, and chest pain. She has never had a kidney stone. She lives far from the hospital, relies on a ride from a neighbor, and says she often cannot get to follow-up appointments.

ROS: Positive for nausea, vomiting, and hematuria. Negative for fever, dysuria, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

Physical Exam: BP 158/90, HR 98, RR 18, Temp 98.6 F, SpO2 99% on room air. Appears uncomfortable and cannot lie still. Abdomen soft with mild right CVA tenderness and no peritoneal signs.

ED Course / Results: Urinalysis showed moderate blood with no nitrite and no leukocytes. Creatinine 1.0. CT abdomen/pelvis without contrast showed a 5 mm obstructing stone at the right ureterovesical junction with mild hydronephrosis. She was given ketorolac 15 mg IV, and her pain improved from 9/10 to 3/10 and the nausea resolved.

Medical Decision Making: Renal colic from a 5 mm right ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis, no signs of infection, and normal renal function. A stone of this size is likely to pass on its own. Pain is controlled and she is tolerating fluids.

Disposition: Discharged home. Ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed with food, strain the urine, and drink plenty of fluids. Because of her transportation barriers, urology will follow up by telephone visit in 1 week, and social work gave her a ride voucher for any in-person visit. Return for fever, uncontrolled pain, or inability to keep fluids down.

Home meds: sertraline 25 mg daily, lorazepam 0.5 mg PRN (uses ~3x/wk), amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily.

CBC: WBC 7.2, Hgb 13.0.
TSH 2.1.

Third episode this month, none this bad, with no clear trigger. Denies SI, HI, AVH, syncope, and fever. No alcohol or drug use; drinks 2 cups of coffee daily. PMH panic disorder for 5 years, HTN, and hypothyroidism. Home meds: sertraline 25 mg daily, lorazepam 0.5 mg PRN about 3 times a week, amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily. Lives alone and her daughter calls daily.
soap.objective: Arrival BP 148/88, HR 112, RR 22, Temp 98.4 F, SpO2 98% RA; after 1 hour HR 84, RR 16, BP 130/78. Anxious and tremulous, speaking fluently, lungs clear, regular rhythm without murmur, no leg edema, neuro nonfocal. MSE: oriented x3, cooperative, anxious affect, linear thought process, no psychosis, no SI or HI, good insight. ECG sinus tachycardia 108 without ST changes, QTc normal; troponin negative x2; BMP normal with K 4.1 and glucose 104; WBC 7.2, Hgb 13.0; TSH 2.1; chest x-ray clear.
soap.assessment: Panic attack in a patient with known panic disorder; medically cleared, with cardiac, pulmonary, and thyroid causes unlikely. Lorazepam use is a fall risk at her age.
plan: Increase sertraline from 25 mg to 50 mg daily
Discontinue lorazepam with no refill
Continue amlodipine and levothyroxine
Outpatient psychiatry referral for CBT
Breathing and relaxation techniques reviewed
Cut back on caffeine
Follow up with PCP in 1 week
Discharge home with daughter; return for chest pain, syncope, or SI
